\chapter{In, On, Under}
\label{ch:mr-in-on-under}
\hlchaptermodality{42}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that a thing is in, on or under a place, running three postpositions off one oblique stem, and I can use var and khālī as bare adverbs when there is no noun to glue them to.}

Complete MR-R42-inside-outside and put a room in, on and under a house from a single bent stem, then say there is something in the room.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[madhye]{\mr{मध्ये} (madhye) — in, inside}

\label{lesson:MR-C42-madhye}



\begin{quote}
Last chapter gave you the oblique stem and the room it was demonstrated on.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{khoolī}, then \emph{khoolīt}, and name what changed — \textbf{nothing}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{मध्ये}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मध्ये}} — \emph{madhye} — \textbf{in, inside, among}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{घरामध्ये} \mr{खोली} \mr{आहे}.} — \emph{gharāmadhye khoolī āhe.} — \textbf{there is a room in the house.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{मध्ये}} and the \textbf{-\mr{त}} you already own do the same job, and Marathi keeps both. \textbf{-\mr{त}} is short and is what speech reaches for; \textbf{\mr{मध्ये}} is longer, unmistakable, and is what a written sign or a form reaches for. A learner who knows only one of them can speak but not read a notice.

Both demand the same oblique stem, which is the point of having met that rule first: \textbf{\mr{घर} $\to$ \mr{घरा}-}, then either ending. Nothing new has to be learned about the noun.

It is Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{मध्य}} (\emph{madhya}), \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{middle}\textquotedblright{} — the same ancient word behind Latin \emph{medius} and English \emph{mid} and \emph{middle}. Its third sense follows from that literally: \textbf{\mr{मध्ये}} also means \emph{among}, in the middle of a group.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{madhye} — in, inside
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{gharāmadhye khoolī āhe}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{-\mr{ल्यावर}} and put an event after coming home
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of \textbf{-\mr{त}} and \textbf{\mr{मध्ये}} would you expect on a printed notice? (\textbf{\mr{मध्ये}}.) What do both demand of the noun first? (\textbf{The oblique stem}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%AE\%E0\%A4\%A7\%E0\%A5\%8D\%E0\%A4\%AF\%E0\%A5\%87}{Wiktionary: \mr{मध्ये}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[var]{\mr{वर} (var) — on, above, up}

\label{lesson:MR-C42-var}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मध्ये}} put something inside. Nothing yet puts something on top.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{वर}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{वर}} — \emph{var} — \textbf{on, above, up}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{घरावर}} — \emph{gharāvar} — \textbf{on the house}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{वर} \mr{पाहा}.} — \emph{var pāhā.} — \textbf{look up.}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{वर}} earns two lessons' worth of use out of one word, and both are worth having now. Glued to an oblique stem it is the \textbf{on} of a surface. Standing alone in front of a verb it is the plain adverb \textbf{up} — no noun needed, and no oblique either, because there is nothing for it to be glued to.

It descends from Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{उपरि}} (\emph{upari}), \textquotedblleft{}above,\textquotedblright{} which is the same ancient word as English \textbf{over} and German \emph{über}. The \emph{up} in \emph{up} is the same syllable.

One more use, and it is the commonest of the three in ordinary speech: Marathi puts affection \textbf{on} its object rather than \emph{for} it.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मी} \mr{मराठीवर} \mr{प्रेम} \mr{करतो}.} — \emph{mī marāṭhīvar prem karto.} — \textbf{I love Marathi.}
\end{quote}

That is not a metaphor you have to decode each time; it is simply where the language puts the thing loved.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{gharāvar} — on the house
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{var pāhā} — look up
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{mī marāṭhīvar prem karto}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \textbf{\mr{सुद्धा}} and add one more thing to that sentence
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
When does \textbf{\mr{वर}} NOT need an oblique stem in front of it? (\textbf{When it stands alone as the adverb \emph{up}.}) What does Marathi put love \emph{on}? (\textbf{The thing loved} — \emph{marāṭhīvar}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%B5\%E0\%A4\%B0}{Wiktionary: \mr{वर}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[khālī]{\mr{खाली} (khālī) — under, below, down}

\label{lesson:MR-C42-khaali}



\begin{quote}
You have \textbf{\mr{वर}}. Every language that has an \emph{on} has an \emph{under}, and in Marathi the two are built the same way.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{खाली}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{खाली}} — \emph{khālī} — \textbf{under, below, down}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{खोलीखाली}} — \emph{khoolīkhālī} — \textbf{under the room}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{खाली} \mr{बसा}.} — \emph{khālī basā.} — \textbf{sit down.}
\end{quote}

Learn it as \textbf{\mr{वर}}'s mirror and you get two facts for one. Glued to an oblique stem it means \textbf{under}; standing alone in front of a verb it is the adverb \textbf{down}. Marathi's up-and-down pair share one grammar, so what you learned about \textbf{\mr{वर}} transfers whole.

\textbf{\mr{खाली} \mr{बसा}} is worth saying aloud twice. It is one of the commonest things a Marathi host says to a guest, and you already own the polite imperative it is built on.

The word is the \textbf{\mr{खाल}} of \emph{underside} with the same \textbf{-\mr{ी}} you saw on \textbf{\mr{खोली}}. Marathi builds a good deal of its everyday vocabulary that way: a short base, a long form, and a job for each.

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{khālī} — under, down
  \item \emph{khālī basā} — sit down
  \item \emph{gharāvar}, then \emph{gharākhālī} — above it, below it
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{\mr{खाली}} do when nothing is glued in front of it? (\textbf{It is the adverb \emph{down}.}) What does a host say to a guest with it? (\textbf{\mr{खाली} \mr{बसा}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%96\%E0\%A4\%BE\%E0\%A4\%B2\%E0\%A5\%80}{Wiktionary: \mr{खाली}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[madhye · var · khālī]{There is a thing, and it is somewhere}

\label{lesson:MR-R42-inside-outside}



\begin{quote}
Three postpositions landed in this chapter and all three sit in the same place. Name them in the order you met them.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{gharāmadhye}, \emph{gharāvar}, \emph{gharākhālī} — and change only the tail
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{khoolīmadhye} — and notice the stem did not move
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{khoolīt kāhī āhe} — there is something in the room
  \item \emph{Recall:} ask \emph{koṇ gharāt āhe?} — who is in the house?
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Marathi has no separate verb for \emph{there is}. What does it use instead? (\textbf{\mr{आहे}}, with a place in front of it.) What has to happen to the noun carrying that place? (\textbf{It takes the oblique stem}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
